Cross Points in a Polygon

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture to explore: drag a point P and the corners of an odd-sided shape, and watch where lines from P cross the opposite sides.
How to play: Drag P or a corner with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Change the number of sides with the buttons, then press Check the claims.
Sides: 5
Look for the math

Choose a shape with an odd number of corners and put a point P anywhere. Join P to every corner. Some of those lines cross the side opposite their own corner: the little orange dots. However you drag P or the corners, the number of dots on the sides is odd, and a product made from the pieces of the sides is exactly 1.

Which side is opposite?

Number the corners A0, A1, and so on. With n corners, the side opposite Am runs from corner Ak to corner Ak+1, where k = m + floor(n/2), counted around the shape. Because n is odd, this pairs things up neatly: if AkAk+1 is opposite Am, then AmAm+1 is opposite Ak+1. The logic test checks this for every odd n from 3 to 21. This is the polygon version of the idea behind Ceva's theorem.

Why an odd number of dots

Move P slowly. A dot leaves its side only by passing an end of that side; that happens exactly when P crosses the diagonal joining the two corners. At that instant two dots change at once — one leaves a side while another arrives, or both leave together. So the count changes by two, and its parity never changes. Far away from the shape there is just one dot, so the count is always odd. The logic test confirms this in thousands of pictures for every odd n from 3 to 21; the count is never even.

The article also says that P outside the shape always gives one dot. That is true when the shape is convex. For a shape with a dent, an outside P can have 3, 5 or more dots — still odd. This page reports that difference plainly instead of hiding it.

Why the product is 1

For the side AkAk+1 and its dot B, measure the two pieces along the direction of the side: AkB / B Ak+1. Count a piece as negative when B is outside the side. Comparing areas of triangles with the same altitude gives

AkB / B Ak+1 = (PAk · sin AkPB) / (PAk+1 · sin B P Ak+1).

Multiply all n fractions. Every length and every sine appears once on top and once below, because the opposite-side pairing works both ways. Everything cancels and the product is 1. Negative fractions come in pairs, which is another way to see the odd count. The logic test compares these fractions with the applet's own line intersection and with an independent area formula on thousands of pictures; the product stays 1 to within a billionth.

When a dot disappears

If P lines up exactly with a corner and the opposite side, the two lines are parallel and have no meeting point. The original applet gets a NaN there; this page simply stops showing that dot and asks you to move a point. The article excludes such positions, and so do the claims above.

Try 21 sides, put P near one corner, and then drag it right through the middle: watch two dots appear or disappear at a time.
